---
title: "convinterp"
subtitle: "High-order convolution interpolation, differentiation, integration and smoothing on grids and scattered data — in Julia and Python"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, CairoMakie
f(x) = cos(x^2 / 9)                                               # a chirp: slow on the left, fast on the right
x_data = range(0, 10, length = 9)                                 # nine samples
y_data = f.(x_data)
x_fine = range(0, 10, length = 1000)

fig = Figure(size = (840, 380))
for (i, (kernels, title)) in enumerate((((:a0, :a1, :a3, :a4, :a5, :a7), "lower-order kernels"),
                                         ((:b5, :b7, :b9, :b11, :b13), "higher-order kernels")))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, i]; title = title, xlabel = "x")
    for k in kernels
        itp = convolution_interpolation(x_data, y_data; kernel = k)   # the interpolant with this kernel
        lines!(ax, x_fine, itp.(x_fine); linewidth = 1.2, label = "kernel = :$k")
    end
    lines!(ax, x_fine, f.(x_fine); color = :black, linewidth = 1.5, label = "true function")
    scatter!(ax, x_data, y_data; markersize = 10, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1.5, label = "samples")
    axislegend(ax; position = :lb, labelsize = 11, rowgap = 0, patchsize = (16, 8))
end
fig
```

convinterp is one method in two languages. Data sampled on a grid, uniform or not, in one
dimension or many, are interpolated by convolution with a piecewise-polynomial kernel; the
interpolant is then differentiated and integrated analytically, or smoothed, or built from
scattered points by fitting the grid to them. The kernels reach 7th-order convergence on uniform
grids and up to 14th on nonuniform ones, with evaluation cost independent of the grid size.

- [**ConvolutionInterpolations.jl**](https://github.com/NikoBiele/ConvolutionInterpolations.jl)
  is the reference implementation, in Julia: every feature on this site, generic over the element
  type, with the kernels stored as exact rationals.
- [**convinterp**](https://github.com/NikoBiele/convinterp) is the Python port, with a Rust core
  and a NumPy interface. It is tested against the Julia package to the last bit of the boundary
  coefficients, and the [feature matrix](features.qmd) says which parts have been ported so far.

The [concept pages](concepts/interpolation.qmd) explain each capability with the same example in
both languages; the [Julia](benchmarks/julia/index.qmd) and [Python](benchmarks/python/index.qmd)
benchmarks compare both packages with the established alternatives in their language, on the same
test functions and with the scripts that produced every figure; and the [theory page](theory.qmd)
derives the kernels from their defining conditions. The Julia package was presented at JuliaCon
2026; the recording is on the [About page](about.qmd).

## Installation

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.add("ConvolutionInterpolations")
```

## Python

```bash
pip install convinterp
```

Prebuilt wheels are available for Linux, macOS and Windows, on x86_64 and ARM.

:::

## A first example

The same data, the same kernel, the same results: a sine sampled at fifty points, interpolated
with the default `b7` kernel and evaluated between the samples, with its derivative and its
integral from the same fifty values.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```julia
using ConvolutionInterpolations

x = range(0, 2π, length = 50)                             # fifty uniformly spaced samples
y = sin.(x)                                               # the values at the samples

itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y)                     # the interpolant, default kernel :b7
d_itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = 1)   # the derivative of the interpolant
i_itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = -1)  # its integral, zero at x = 0

itp(1.0), d_itp(1.0), i_itp(1.0)                          # evaluate between the samples
```

| | f(1) | f′(1) | ∫₀¹ f |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| from fifty samples | 0.841470984879974 | 0.540302305515489 | 0.459697694147643 |
| exact | 0.841470984807897 | 0.540302305868140 | 0.459697694131860 |

## Python

```python
import numpy as np
from convinterp import convolution_interpolation

x = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 50)                       # fifty uniformly spaced samples
y = np.sin(x)                                             # the values at the samples

itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y)                     # the interpolant, default kernel "b7"
d_itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=1)     # the derivative of the interpolant
i_itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-1)    # its integral, zero at x = 0

itp(1.0), d_itp(1.0), i_itp(1.0)                          # evaluate between the samples
```

| | f(1) | f′(1) | ∫₀¹ f |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| from fifty samples | 0.841470984879974 | 0.540302305515489 | 0.459697694147643 |
| exact | 0.841470984807897 | 0.540302305868140 | 0.459697694131860 |

:::

Ten correct digits from fifty samples per period; the point of the kernels is that the error
keeps falling as the 7th power of the spacing as samples are added — the
[interpolation benchmark](benchmarks/julia/interpolation.qmd) shows the curve.

## Status

ConvolutionInterpolations.jl is at version 1 and its interface is stable. convinterp is an alpha
release: what it has is tested against the reference, and what it lacks is listed on the
[feature matrix](features.qmd).
